items.abstract: <jats:p>Retail forecasting models that see the price and promotion plan can explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift each part of the plan adds. Merchants read that split as fact and plan on it. We set out eight checks on such explanations, fixed in advance: properties that hold by construction, sensitivity to randomised weights, stability across seeds, price direction, agreement with what sold, agreement with LightGBM, a plan read-back, and agreement with a measured cause. In generated store data with known effects, a world model whose explanation is built in passes C1 and C3 to C6, and its lifts match the truth (rank agreement 0.99) when plans are made at random. When merchants plan into high-demand weeks, it still passes them, forecasts more accurately, and overstates the total lift by a third (1.33 to 1.40 times) and the display's by 1.81 to 1.93 times; LightGBM overstates them too, and the two agree. Asked about a lasting change in the regular price, the world model answers with the temporary-cut response,-2.42 to-2.37 against a true-0.5, and only the measured cause finds it. The price-direction check catches every model blind to price but also flags LightGBM; an exploratory lever-by-lever comparison catches lifts given to the wrong lever; the randomisation check separates nothing. On Dominick's we find 54 spells in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers, most between April 1993 and April 1994. Over the 38 scored spells, prices 6% to 10% off their peers, the pooled effect on category units is-0.33 over eight weeks (95% interval-0.68 to 0.01) and-0.52 over the full spell (-0.81 to-0.23), in line with the elasticity near-0.3 the chain's experiments implied. This is a noisy observational benchmark, not a ground truth: the treated stores are inferred, prices move before the detected start, and a placebo at false start dates gives-0.26 (-0.72 to 0.19), close to the 8-week estimate. We then audited all 494 saved world-model and lift-model versions of our companion paper on M5, Dominick's and Breakfast at the Frat. With C1 scored against the audit's own plan for nothing planned, no version passed every check on M5 or Dominick's; with C1 read against each model's own plan, which removes failures of the audit's interface rather than of the models, none did on M5 and 6 of 540 Dominick's version-windows did, the rest failing other checks, most often price direction. The baseline and lift add up to the forecast in every version, and under the model's own plan for nothing planned the lift is zero; under the audit's plan it was not, on most Dominick's and Frat versions, and every such failure sits where the two plans differ: some configurations take the regular price from a held or recorded price, and for items with no recent price the models compute the baseline at the item's mean price or at 1.0. On Dominick's and M5 a deeper price cut lowered the forecast in about half the itemweeks or more; and on M5 the lifts agreed poorly between seeds although the forecasts agreed. Both models state about twice the measured response to the zone price deviations, though the measured interval is wide and overlaps both. Comparing configurations on the same data and window, resampling whole configurations, the number of checks passed was not clearly related to accuracy (pooled Spearman-0.10, 95% interval-0.21 to 0.02); with C5, which compares the forecast with sales, left out,-0.02 (-0.13 to 0.12). These results hold for these models and data sets.</jats:p>
title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Causal Validity
